## Methods

Materials
All chemicals and reagents were of analytical grade and were used as received. The 1,2-dichlorobenzene (o-DCB, 99%), anhydrous n-butanol (99.4%), dioxane (99%), mesitylene (99%), and pyrrolidine (Py, 98%) were sourced from Macklin Chemicals. 2,4,6-tris(4-aminophenyl)triazine (TP, 97%), 4,4″-diamino-substituted p-terphenyl (SB, >97.0%), 4,4′-(benzo-2,1,3-thiadiazole-4,7-diyl)dianiline (BT-0F, 98%), and benzene-1,3,5-tricarbaldehyde (BTA, >98.0%) were obtained from Jilin Chinese Academy of Sciences-Yanshen Technology Co. Ltd.

Characterization
PXRD patterns were collected on a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer using Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.54 Å) operated at 45 kV and 35 mA. FT-IR spectra were acquired with a Thermo Fisher Nicolet Avatar 6700 FT-IR spectrometer. UV-Vis absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV-2700 spectrophotometer. Nitrogen sorption isotherms were measured at 77 K using an iPore 400 analyzer. Prior to measurement, samples were degassed at 120°C under dynamic vacuum (<10−3 Torr) for 10 h. Specific surface areas were determined using the BET method, and pore size distributions were derived from the sorption isotherms via NLDFT. XPS was performed on a VG ESCALAB 250 system. TEM was carried out on a JEOL JEM-2010 instrument. The piezoelectric response was characterized by PFM using a Bruker Dimension Icon atomic force microscope. Photo-enhanced KPFM measurements were conducted using an AFM system equipped with an SKPM module and a xenon lamp source.

Piezo-photocatalytic H2 and H2O2 evolution
The photocatalytic reaction was conducted in a 40 mL cylindrical optical reactor (outer diameter: 27.5 mm, height: 95 mm) containing 2 mg of catalyst dispersed in 20 mL of ultrapure water. The suspension was simultaneously irradiated with a 300 W Xe lamp (CEL-PF300-T9, Beijing Zhongjiao Jinyuan) and ultrasonicated (JP101T cleaner, 40 kHz, 60 W; Shenzhen Jiemen). The lamp was equipped with a visible light cut-off filter (λ≥420 nm) to provide an incident light intensity of 1000 W m−2, as calibrated by a solar power meter (Model SM206-SOLAR). The reaction temperature was maintained at 20.0 ± 0.5°C by a circulating cooling water system.

Prior to reaction, the system was purged by three alternating cycles of evacuation and argon purging (each 5 min) to ensure an anaerobic environment. During the reaction, 100 μL of headspace gas was periodically extracted with a gas-tight syringe for hydrogen analysis by gas chromatography (GC, FULI GC9790 PLF-01, FULI instruments) equipped with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The H2 yield was determined using a standard calibration curve (Fig. S69A).

The concentration of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) was quantified via an enzymatic method using horseradish peroxidase (HRP) to catalyze the reaction between H2O2 and 3,3’,5,5’-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB).

The piezo-photocatalytic production of H2 and H2O2 was investigated under varying ultrasonic intensities and frequencies. The experiments employed a multi-frequency ultrasonic cleaner (YNLH0203-204060, Shenzhen Yunyi) with selectable frequencies (20, 40, 60 kHz) and corresponding powers (30, 60, 120 W). All other conditions were consistent with those described above.

Measurement of H2O2
The H2O2 concentration was quantified using a 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB)-based enzymatic assay, in which horseradish peroxidase (HRP) catalyzes the oxidation of TMB by H2O2.

The TMB stock solution was prepared by first dissolving 15 mg of TMB in 0.3 mL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). This solution was then mixed with 5 mL of glycerol and 45 mL of an aqueous solution containing 20 mg of ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and 95 mg of citric acid. The mixture was finally diluted to a total volume of 500 mL with deionized water. The HRP solution was prepared by dissolving 2 mg of the enzyme in 10 mL of deionized water.

For the calibration, 200 μL of the TMB solution and 10 μL of the HRP solution were added to a known concentration of H2O2 (100 μL). After 3 min of reaction, HCl (10 μL, 12 M) was added to stop the reaction, and the absorbance at 450 nm was measured by UV-Vis spectroscopy. A linear standard curve was established from these measurements and used to determine the H2O2 concentration in the experimental samples. The testing method for the actual samples was identical to that used for the reference standard. The H2O2 yield was calculated based on these calibration curves (Fig. S69B, C).

Apparent quantum yields (AQYs) measurements
Apparent quantum yields (AQYs) were determined using 5 mg of samples dispersed in 20 mL of water, with a 300 W Xe lamp (CEL-PF300-T9, Beijing Zhongjiao Jinyuan Technology Co., Ltd.) equipped with band-pass filters (λ=450, 500, 550, 600 and 650 nm) as the incident light source (irradiation area: 0.25 cm2), under the combined conditions of irradiation and ultrasonic assistance for 30 min. The light intensity was measured with a solar power meter (Model SM206-SOLAR). The AQY was calculated using the following formula (1):

η = (2 × M × NA × h × c) / (S × P × t × λ) × 100% (1)

Where M is the amount of H2 produced (mol), NA is the Avogadro constant (6.022 × 1023/mol), h is the Planck constant (6.626 × 10−34 Js), c is the speed of light (3 × 108 m/s), S is the irradiation area of the incident light (m2), P is the intensity of the incident light (W/m2), t is the photoreaction time (s), and λ is the wavelength of the monochromatic light (m).

By substituting the known constants, we obtained the following simplified formula (2) for the AQY:

η = (2 × M × 2.66 × 109) / (P × λ) × 100% (2)

Where M is the amount of H2 produced (mol), P is the intensity of the incident light (W/m2), and λ is the wavelength of the monochromatic light (nm). Specific values are provided in Table S14.

Trapping experiments of hydroxyl radicals
An aqueous terephthalic acid (TA) solution (40 mL, 0.5 mM) was formulated in a 2 mM NaOH medium and then transferred into a quartz reactor. A 5 mg portion of the photocatalyst was uniformly dispersed in the aforementioned solution. The resulting mixture was exposed to visible light irradiation (300 W Xe lamp, λ>420 nm, light intensity: 1000 W/m2) for 1 h at 20°C under constant magnetic stirring. Following the irradiation process, the suspension was subjected to centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 10 min. The fluorescence emission intensity of the supernatant was determined at 425 nm (excitation wavelength: 315 nm) via a fluorescence spectrometer.

Piezo-photoelectrochemical measurements
Piezo-photoelectrochemical measurements were performed using a standard three-electrode setup on a CHI660E electrochemical workstation, under visible light (λ≥420 nm) and ultrasonic irradiation. The working electrode was prepared by dispersing 2 mg of catalyst in a mixture of 0.5 mL ethanol and 10 μL Nafion solution, followed by sonication for 5 min to obtain a homogeneous suspension. Next, 50 μL of the suspension was drop-cast onto a pre-cleaned ITO glass substrate (0.5 × 0.5 cm2) fixed with double-sided tape. A proton exchange membrane (1 × 1 cm2) was then placed on the catalyst-coated region and hot-pressed at 100°C under 350 psi pressure for 3 min, thereby forming the working electrode (Fig. S70).

Mott-Schottky analysis was carried out using a three-electrode configuration, where the COF/ITO glass served as the working electrode, a platinum (Pt) plate functioned as the counter electrode, and a saturated Ag/AgCl electrode acted as the reference. The electrolyte consisted of 30 mL deionized water with 0.20 M Na2SO4. This study involved applying a polarization potential from −1.2 to 1.6 V (vs. SCE), with alternating potential frequencies of 500, 1000, and 1500 Hz employed throughout the study.

Photocurrent tests were conducted under the conditions of irradiation, sonication, or their simultaneous application. EIS tests were conducted at a bias voltage of −0.4 V, covering irradiation, sonication, or their combined action, with a frequency range of 0.001–100000 Hz. For EIS tests performed under ultrasound, the electrochemical cell was secured in an ultrasonic bath. The acquired EIS data were fitted with a suitable equivalent circuit17.

In situ high-pressure PL, IR, and UV-Vis absorption measurements
High-pressure experiments utilized a symmetric diamond anvil cell (DAC) (Fig. S71) equipped with ultra-low fluorescence diamond anvils (culet diameter: 400 μm). Samples were loaded into a 150 μm-diameter chamber laser-drilled in a pre-indented T301 stainless steel gasket (thickness: 45 μm), with silicon oil (PL/UV-Vis) or KBr (IR) selected as pressure-transmitting media. The ruby fluorescence technique was utilized for pressure determination, relying on the spectral shift of the R1 line in ruby fluorescence. All the aforementioned measurements were performed at 298 K.

Spectroscopic measurements. Photoluminescence (PL): excited with a 355 nm semiconductor laser (with power stabilized to avoid intensity-related artifacts), and the corresponding spectra were collected by an Ocean Optics QE65000 fiber spectrometer (Fig. S72).

UV-Vis absorption: a deuterium-halogen excitation source was coupled to the same spectrometer, with a focus on excitonic absorption bands (Fig. S73).

Infrared (IR): recorded using a Nicolet iN10 microscope spectrometer (equipped with a liquid N2-cooled MCT detector), where KBr was used as the pressure-transmitting medium (Fig. S74).

In situ EPR monitoring experiments
EPR spectra were recorded at 298 K using a Magnettech ESR 5000 spectrometer (X-band, 9.85 GHz) (Fig. S75) with the adoption of the following instrumental parameters: modulation amplitude of 1.000 G, modulation frequency of 100 kHz, center field of 3500 G, and sweep width of 100 G. For in situ radical detection, 10 mg of the COF composite was dispersed in 20 mL of an aqueous solution supplemented with 200 μL of 0.1 M DMPO as the spin trap, and then exposed to simultaneous ultrasonic treatment (40 kHz, 60 W) and visible-light irradiation (300 W Xe lamp, λ≥420 nm) in a 40 mL quartz reactor. The resulting reaction mixture was continuously circulated through the EPR sample cell by a peristaltic pump at a flow rate of 6 mL/min, facilitating real-time detection at 30-s intervals.

High piezoelectric coefficient (d33) test
The powder sample was subjected to a pressure of 4 tons for tableting to prepare a flake-shaped specimen, which was then placed in an oil bath for polarization treatment. The polarization conditions were as follows: the polarization voltage was 1400 V, the leakage current was controlled at 0.05 mA, the polarization temperature was room temperature, and the polarization duration was set to 0.5 h. The test sample was further tested between the upper and lower probes. The electromagnetic drive part in the test head generated a low-frequency alternating force of approximately 0.25 N at a frequency of 110 Hz. The two piezoelectric signals generated by the positive piezoelectric effect were then processed by the instrument, which displayed the d33 value.

Calculation method
All DFT calculations in this work were calculated with the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP, version 6.3.0), implemented with plane waves and the projector augmented wave method. The Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) functionals were coupled with van der Waals (vdW) dispersion corrections of the zero-damping DFT-D3 method of Grimme51,52. All structures of these COFs (see Supplementary Data 1–4) were optimized until all Hellmann-Feynman forces on atoms were less than 0.005 eV/Å with cell optimization and an energy cutoff of 550 eV and a Γ-centered k-mesh with a k-point distance of <2π/36 Å−1. The piezoelectric tensors, effective Born charges of these COFs were determined from the response to finite electric fields (E=0.001 eV/Å). Geometry optimizations and electronic structure characterizations of the molecules were performed at the B3LYP/6-311G level using the Gaussian 1653. Our DFT calculations employed idealized COF models, which cannot fully capture the inherent structural complexity and dynamic nature of the real systems.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors present a promising approach to boosting piezo-photocatalytic water splitting through strategic dipole moment engineering in β-ketoenamine/imine-linked covalent organic frameworks (COFs). By precisely controlling molecular architecture, they developed TP-BT-0F-COF, demonstrating remarkable piezoelectric coefficients and record-breaking H2/H2O2 generation rates under simultaneous ultrasound and light irradiation. This study systematically establishes the relationship between dipole moment manipulation, piezoelectric polarization, and catalytic performance, revealing the crucial influence of symmetry-disrupted benzothiadiazole moieties and in-plane polarization of ketoenamine linkages. DFT calculations further pinpoint N⁸ and C⁶ as active catalytic sites, providing robust mechanistic understanding. Representing a major leap in mechano-optical energy conversion, this work offers a molecular-level design strategy for multifunctional COF catalysts. The comprehensive experimental evidence combined with theoretical analysis delivers deep insights into dipole-mediated piezoelectric enhancement. The work is recommended for publication in Nature Communications after addressing minor revisions:
1. The observed discrepancy between the solid-state UV-Vis absorption spectrum (Figure 1C) and the calculated bandgap (Figure 1D) necessitates either re-evaluation of the experimental measurements or revision of the computational methodology.
2. Regarding the Figures shown in the article, some logical or formatting issues are pointed out as follows: 1) Figures 1C and 1D show that the bandgap of TP-SB-COF is the largest among the involved COF materials. However, a rough analysis of the UV absorption spectra indicates a contradiction between this conclusion and the information presented in the spectra; 2) The pressure values in Figure 2 have inconsistent decimal places and need to be standardized
3. In Figure 4D and Figure S55, the Nyquist plots of the EIS should be fitted with appropriate equivalent circuits in order to allow for a quantitative analysis of the interface resistance.
4. More citations should be added to provide readers with a more comprehensive background on the application of crystalline porous materials in piezoelectric photocatalysis. Some references: 10.1002/adma.202419023, 10.1002/anie.202419867, 10.1002/adma.202106308, 10.1038/s41467-024-53834-w, 10.1002/anie.202420218.
5. This study systematically investigates the piezo-photocatalytic performance of dipole-engineered COFs. However, the dipole moment calculations appear limited to the TP-based COF series (TP-BT-0F-COF, TP-BT-1F-COF, TP-BT-2F-COF, TP-SB-COF), while omitting the BTA-BT-0F-COF counterpart. Could the authors clarify: 1) The scientific rationale for selectively calculating dipole moments only for TP-based frameworks? 2) Whether the dipole moment analysis was conducted for BTA-BT-0F-COF, and if not, whether its exclusion might influence the established structure-property relationships?
6. Elaborate on the light-only experimental configuration, specifying whether agitation (e.g., magnetic stirring) was employed during the illumination period. Include a control experiment featuring stirring in the absence of light to decouple mechanical effects from photochemical contributions. Further distinguish the roles of ultrasound and mechanical stirring by clarifying their distinct influences on reaction kinetics-such as cavitation effects for ultrasound versus bulk mixing for mechanical stirring-to precisely define the action mechanisms of different energy inputs.

### Reviewer 3

Liu and co-workers have demonstrated photo-piezocatalytic water splitting using covalent organic frameworks (COFs), in their work entitled- “Enhanced piezo-photocatalytic water splitting activity via engineering robust dipole moments in covalent organic frameworks”. The study is interesting, especially since photo-piezocatalysis in COFs has been rarely documented. However, there are major experimental concerns that the authors must address.
Please find the comments given here.
1. The biggest drawback of the work is perhaps the fact that no experimental evidence has been provided in the manuscript to confirm the non-centrosymmetric structure of the COFs utilised in the study. The authors state that the COFs crystallize in P-1 space group which is a centrosymmetric space group. The authors should re-evaluate the space groups of the materials used from their Pawley refinement patterns and provide additional proof for non-centrosymmetry with experiments like second harmonic generation. Please refer to and cite these recent related papers for these analyses: Chem. Mater. 2021, 33, 818, Adv. Funct. Mater. 2025, 2502787, ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853. Additionally, the framework structures seem planar and symmetric. The authors must explain why and how symmetry breaking occurs in the framework, giving rise to piezoelectric polarization.
2. The PFM studies need to be rechecked. For an artifact free dataset, the switching potentials observed for the phase loop and amplitude loop should match. In this case, in the positive region, the potentials do not match, which raises significant concern regarding the contribution of charging or electrochemical reactions to the PFM data. Please check relevant references: Nat. Commun., 2019, 10, 1661, Adv. Mater. 2022, 34, 2206237. Also, the authors don’t mention whether the provided data is the ‘off-state’ or ‘on-state’ data. Also, the sentence, “From the amplitude loop, TP-BT-0F-COF had an amplitude of 3.0 nm” doesn’t quite make much sense. The authors should evaluate the piezoelectric coefficient of the materials from the amplitude data following previous reports.
3. The authors should explore the photo-piezocatalytic activity in more detail. Analyses must be done by varying the ultrasonication power and frequency to check the catalytic activity. Furthermore, the apparent quantum efficiency of the process must be evaluated under a single ultrasonication frequency (preferably the best one) by varying the light wavelength. The synergy % of the photo- and piezocatalytic processes must be evaluated and compared.
4. Isotope labelling experiments for both the redox halves need to be carried out to confirm the origin of the products. The authors should also carry out charge trapping experiments for both the redox halves. Please refer to: Nano Lett. 2022, 22, 8867, Adv. Funct. Mater. 2025, 2502787.
5. KPFM gives an idea of the surface potential of a material which is also often correlated with its surface charge and work function. The authors claim that TP-BT-0F-COF exhibited a surface potential of 68 mV in the dark, which decreased to -30mV upon exposure to light due to the effect of the inward piezoelectric potential field. This is rather surprising. A strong justification with suitable references must be provided. A decrease can be anticipated but such a huge difference with charge in potential sign seems difficult. Also, the topography image of KPFM should reflect the topography/height of the material. The image presented in Fig. 4E shows a rather flat, blank surface with no material present.
6. In Fig. 4B-D, how do the authors make sure that the material coating doesn’t come off the electrode surface upon rigorous ultrasonication?
7. Finally, the authors should comment on the ferroic properties of the materials used. Are they ferroelectric, piezoelectric, or ferrielectric? What is the mechanism behind their piezo-tunable dipole generation? These are crucial aspects to be looked at for photo-piezocatalyst design, especially in emerging materials like COFs.
Based on all these concerns, I am unable to recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications.

### Reviewer 4

The authors Liang et al. synthesized four COFs based on the monomer 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol (TP) and applied them for piezoelectric photocatalytic overall water splitting to produce H2 and H2O2. I do not recommend this paper for publication in Nature Communications, and I will elaborate on my reasons through the following points:
1. Innovation: In the introduction, the authors state that "classical inorganic piezoelectric materials are limited by poor structural tunability and complex polarization processes, which severely hamper their mechanically driven catalytic efficiency," while highlighting the advantages of COFs. They also note recent reports on piezoelectric COFs. However, their core innovation claim—"current research lacks systematic tuning of COF ligand structures to modulate dipole moments and establish polarization centers, which are essential for achieving precise piezoelectric control"—is invalid.
Multiple studies have already addressed these aspects:
• Li et al. (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218) demonstrated how ethenyl, F, Br, and OMe groups modulate dipole moments and piezoelectric of COFs.
• Gu et al. (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202409708) constructed piezoelectric COFs using fluorinated alkyl chains and investigated the effects of benzene rings and triazine groups on dipole moments and piezoelectric properties.
• Chen et al. (ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853−7866) synthesized two piezoelectric conjugated microporous polymers (CMPs) with Zn-Salen, discussing similar structural influences. Notably, their Zn-Salen-TEPT and Zn-Salen-TEPB systems achieved higher H2 and H2O2 production rates than the authors' COFs under ultrasound alone. (Note: When COFs lose crystallinity, they become conjugated porous polymers; thus, comparison with CMPs is valid.).
Additional examples of ligand structure tuning in organic frameworks include: Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2106308; Chem. Commun. 2025, 61, 2536–2539; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202425656; ChemCatChem 2025, 17, e202402105; Chem. Eng. J. 512 (2025) 162529, et. al. Thus, the authors' claim that "current research lacks systematic tuning of COF ligand structures" is unsupported.
Side Notes:
• Reference 21 is unrelated to piezoelectricity but is cited to support piezoelectric COFs.
• References 23–24, while piezoelectric, do not substantiate the authors' assertion that "These elements are essential for achieving precise piezoelectric control.
• The authors’ assertion in the abstract claiming "outperforming state-of-the-art COF-based piezo-photocatalysts" lacks supporting evidence. For reference, the following studies demonstrate superior performance: ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853–7866; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 64, e202419867. These works already report COF-based or related systems with higher catalytic efficiency, further undermining the novelty and competitiveness of the authors’ claims.
Regarding the second innovation claim—"establish polarization centers"—the authors themselves previously attributed the piezoelectricity of EA-COF to the in-plane polarization of TP groups in ACS Catal. 14, 10447–10461 (2024). The current work fails to provide new insights beyond reiterating this phenomenon.
While the authors conducted extensive experimental work, the paper lacks significant original innovation. I will now address technical concerns in subsequent sections.
2. Technical:
1. Numerous studies have demonstrated that introducing fluorine (F) to modulate dipole moments in organic materials often results in positive regulation.
Dipole moments quantify the degree of charge separation between positive and negative charges, reflecting asymmetry in charge distribution at molecular or atomic scales. Mathematically, the dipole moment (μ) is defined as:
μ= q⋅d, where q is the charge magnitude and d is the displacement vector from the negative to the positive charge.
The authors’ DFT computational model adopts a symmetric structure centered on the BT molecule. However, since their ligand modifications are solely based on the BT moiety, the inherent symmetry of this design diminishes the impact of molecular adjustments. For instance, in TP-SB-COF, the dipole moments from opposing sides are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, leading to negligible overall dipole moments in DFT calculations (Fig. 1). Using the molecular fragment within the red box in Figure 2 (one TP molecule connected to three BT molecules) for calculations can avoid the aforementioned issues.
Fig.1 Dipole polarization ability of TP-SB-COF
Fig.2 The recommended molecular fragment model for dipole polarization
2. The water oxidation reaction to produce H2O2 should involve quenching ·OH radicals, not holes (h⁺).
3. While terephthalic acid is widely used to detect ·OH radicals, its instability under light-ultrasound conditions compromises reliability. Additionally, the authors claim: "This may be because the COFs reduced the residual oxygen in the water to H2O2." This introduces ambiguity in experimental reproducibility and challenges the validity of ·OH detection via terephthalic acid. Proper control experiments, such as isotopic labeling with H218O, are critical to confirm that H2O2 originates from water oxidation rather than oxygen reduction.
4. Lacking cyclic tests and characterization of the materials after reaction.
5. Powdered materials cannot be directly tested for d33 coefficients using standard d33 meters. Supplementary Fig. S37 merely displays a photograph without detailing sample preparation or measurement protocols.
6. The authors employed diamond anvil cells for characterization, but it remains unclear whether such extreme pressure conditions are relevant to practical piezoelectric catalysis. While similar methods are used in piezofluorochromism studies (e.g., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, e202409099), the connection between these fields and piezoelectric catalysis remains unexplained.
3. Conclusion
The paper suffers from insufficient innovation and logical rigor. Based on the above analysis, I do not recommend this paper for publication in Nature Communications.

(1) Isotopic Labeling Confirms Product Origins:
(a) Reduction Half-Reaction (H Origin):
Deuterium labeling experiments utilizing D O (98%) as the solvent unequivocally demonstrated that H originates from the reduction of water. Mass spectrometry revealed a distinct molecular ion peak at m/z = 4.00 (Fig. S56), corresponding to D evolution, thereby providing irrefutable confirmation of the proton reduction pathway.
(b) Oxidation Half-Reaction (H O and •OH Origins):
In order to investigate the water oxidation pathway, H 18O was employed as the reaction medium. The oxidation of benzoic acid produced p-hydroxybenzoic acid (p-HBA), with a characteristic mass peak at m/z = 139.0296 (Fig. S60). This signal corresponds to the 18O-labeled p-HBA adduct, substantiating that •OH radicals (and thus H O ) are derived from water oxidation. The reaction sequence is as follows: (H O + h+ → •OH + H+, 2.32 V vs NHE; 2•OH → H O , 0.74 V vs NHE)
(2) Charge Trapping Experiments Elucidate Redox Pathways:
To distinguish the roles of electrons and holes in the redox processes, scavenger-assisted studies were carried out:
(a) Electron Trapping (Reduction Suppression):
The addition of 10 mM AgNO (electron scavenger) led to a 90% suppression of H evolution, affirming that H production is governed by electron-driven proton reduction.
(b) Hole Trapping and •OH Quenching (Oxidation Suppression):
Hole Scavenging: The introduction of 10 mM EDTA-2Na reduced H O yield by 87%, confirming that holes initiate the water oxidation step.
•OH Quenching: The addition of 10 vol% tert-butanol (TBA) resulted in an 91% decrease in H O production, further corroborating the dominance of •OH coupling in H O formation. These findings are in harmony with in situ ESR data (Fig. S59), where •OH signals were exclusively observed under piezo-photocatalytic conditions (ultrasound and light), but were absent under light alone.
(3) Summary of Mechanistic Insights
These integrated experiments provide definitive evidence that: H originates from water reduction via electron-mediated proton reduction. H O forms through an indirect two-step water oxidation process involving hole-generated •OH radicals. Piezoelectric fields are indispensable for activating the water oxidation reaction (WOR) pathway, as corroborated by isotopic labeling (in situ ESR and MS) and charge-trapping kinetics.

(1) Clarification of Piezoelectric Properties:
The piezoelectricity of the synthesized COFs has been comprehensively confirmed through multiple characterization methods. Specifically, piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) measurements reveal switchable polarization behavior under a ±5 V bias, accompanied by a 180° phase reversal (Fig. 2A, S31), directly demonstrating their piezoelectric activity. Quasi-static measurements further verify high piezoelectric coefficients, with TP-BT-0F-COF exhibiting a d value of 5.5 pC/N (Fig. S37). Additionally, the presence of second harmonic generation (SHG) signals at 700 nm (Fig. S38A) and the violation of infrared (IR)/Raman mutual exclusion rules (Fig. S38B) collectively confirm the non-centrosymmetric structure of these COFs-a structural prerequisite for piezoelectricity. These results systematically validate the piezoelectric nature of the materials.
(2) Ferroelectric or Ferrielectric (Excluded):
The materials were confirmed to lack ferroelectric and ferrielectric properties through systematic characterizations. Specifically, no hysteresis or remnant polarization was observed in the polarization-electric field (P-E) loops (As shown in the Figure R1 below), which directly rules out ferroelectric behavior. Additionally, polarization switching in PFM measurements is instantaneous and reversible, devoid of the characteristic hysteresis associated with ferroelectrics. For ferrielectricity, no evidence supporting this property was found either: there is no indication of antiparallel dipole domains or sub-lattice polarization asymmetry-features typical of ferrielectric materials. These results collectively demonstrate that the materials do not exhibit ferroelectric or ferrielectric behavior.
Reviewer 4:
The authors Liang et al. synthesized four COFs based on the monomer 1,3,5-triformylphloroglucinol (TP) and applied them for piezoelectric photocatalytic overall water splitting to produce H and H O . I do not recommend this paper for publication in Nature Communications, and I will elaborate on my reasons through the following points:
1. Innovation: In the introduction, the authors state that ‘classical inorganic piezoelectric materials are limited by poor structural tunability and complex polarization processes, which severely hamper their mechanically driven catalytic efficiency,’ while highlighting the advantages of COFs. They also note recent reports on piezoelectric COFs. However, their core innovation claim- ‘current research lacks systematic tuning of COF ligand structures to modulate dipole moments and establish polarization centers, which are essential for achieving precise piezoelectric control’-is invalid.
Multiple studies have already addressed these aspects:
• Li et al. (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218) demonstrated how ethenyl, F, Br, and OMe groups modulate dipole moments and piezoelectric of COFs.
• Gu et al. (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202409708) constructed piezoelectric COFs using fluorinated alkyl chains and investigated the effects of benzene rings and triazine groups on dipole moments and piezoelectric properties.
• Chen et al. (ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853-7866) synthesized two piezoelectric conjugated microporous polymers (CMPs) with Zn-Salen, discussing similar structural influences. Notably, their Zn-Salen-TEPT and Zn-Salen-TEPB systems achieved higher H and H O production rates than the authors’ COFs under ultrasound alone. (Note: When COFs lose crystallinity, they become conjugated porous polymers; thus, comparison with CMPs is valid.).
Additional examples of ligand structure tuning in organic frameworks include: Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2106308; Chem. Commun. 2025, 61, 2536-2539; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202425656; ChemCatChem 2025, 17, e202402105; Chem. Eng. J. 512 (2025) 162529, et. al. Thus, the authors’ claim that ‘current research lacks systematic tuning of COF ligand structures’ is unsupported.
Side Notes:
• Reference 21 is unrelated to piezoelectricity but is cited to support piezoelectric COFs.
• References 23-24, while piezoelectric, do not substantiate the authors' assertion that "These elements are essential for achieving precise piezoelectric control.
• The authors’ assertion in the abstract claiming "outperforming state-of-the-art COF-based piezo-photocatalysts" lacks supporting evidence. For reference, the following studies demonstrate superior performance: ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853-7866; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218; Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 64, e202419867. These works already report COF-based or related systems with higher catalytic efficiency, further undermining the novelty and competitiveness of the authors’ claims.
Regarding the second innovation claim-"establish polarization centers"-the authors themselves previously attributed the piezoelectricity of EA-COF to the in-plane polarization of TP groups in ACS Catal. 14, 10447-10461 (2024). The current work fails to provide new insights beyond reiterating this phenomenon.
While the authors conducted extensive experimental work, the paper lacks significant original innovation. I will now address technical concerns in subsequent sections.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's valuable comments, which provide important insights for refining our work. Regarding the concerns raised about the innovation of our research, we offer the following clarifications to highlight the distinctive aspects of our study.
(1) Statement on Innovation
(a) Context of Piezoelectric Framework Literature
We acknowledge the reviewer's attention to relevant piezoelectric material studies. Concerning the cited literature on piezoelectric COFs, we note that currently only three reports (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202409708, ACS Catal. 14, 10447-10461 (2024)) exist:
Two reports focus on applications distinct from our work.
The third report is a prior publication from our own research group.
Additionally, one related study exists on piezoelectric conjugated microporous polymers (CMPs).
(b) Distinction from Other Framework Materials (MOFs)
The cited framework materials by reviewer (Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2106308, Chem. Commun. 2025, 61, 2536-2539, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202425656, ChemCatChem 2025, 17, e202402105, Chem. Eng. J. 512 (2025) 162529, et. al.) primarily involve MOFs. While MOFs share the ‘framework’ designation with COFs, they differ fundamentally in design principles and structural characteristics-notably in their linkage chemistry, crystallinity, and organic-inorganic composition. Consequently, the structural regulation strategies and piezoelectric mechanisms observed in MOFs are not directly transferable to COF-based systems. Our work is explicitly centered on COF-specific structural engineering, representing a distinct research focus within piezoelectric framework materials.
(2) Specific Analysis of Cited Articles
We have analyzed the three key piezoelectric COF articles identified by the reviewer – the only relevant studies to date.
(Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218): This work employs twisted bicarbazole groups to achieve non-centrosymmetry for piezo-photocatalysis. Crucially, its core building blocks, topology, and dipole modulation principles (focusing on group twistability) are fundamentally different from our COF structure and modification strategy (focused on dipole moment magnitude via element substitution). The universality discussion of bicarbazole groups does not involve deep comparison of dipole moments or overlap with our element modification approach.
(Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 63, e202409708): This study utilizes fluorinated alkyl chains on imine-linked COFs to induce non-centrosymmetry for piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs). Its structural design (side-chain functionalization) and application target (PENGs) are unrelated to the core focus of our work. It serves as complementary evidence for the potential of piezoelectric COFs rather than conflicting with our innovation.
(ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853-7866 - CMP): This research investigates donor-acceptor (D-A) structured CMPs for piezo-catalytic water splitting. Being a polymer material (CMP) with a different structure and dipole modulation mechanism (D-A architecture), it does not pertain directly to crystalline COFs or our specific structural engineering approach. Its existence further supports the broader field but does not overlap with the novelty presented in our study.
Conclusion on Innovation:
In summary, the cited studies employ distinct methodologies (twisted groups, fluorinated side-chains, D-A polymers) to achieve piezoelectricity, differing fundamentally in their structural design, modification strategy, application focus, and/or material class (CMP) from our work. Our research introduces a novel and specific approach to piezoelectric COF design based on targeted element substitution within the core COF backbone to modulate dipole moment magnitude, addressing a unique aspect of COF structural engineering. Therefore, we believe the core innovation and contribution of our work remain valid and distinct.
(3) Clarification on Innovation: Polarization Centers and Novelty
We appreciate the opportunity to further elaborate on our core innovation regarding polarization centers and material design:
(a) Advancing beyond Prior Work
While polarization centers were previously proposed via theoretical calculations, this study provides experimental validation through in situ high pressure techniques, offering deeper mechanistic insights.
(b) First Introduction of BT Groups in Piezo-Photocatalysis
Our work pioneers the strategic incorporation of benzothiadiazole (BT) functional groups into COFs for piezo-photocatalysis. This enables: Construction of non-centrosymmetric frameworks via BT’s inherent asymmetry, Precise dipole moment modulation through BT’s electron-withdrawing nature, enhancing polarization of TP units.
(c) Novel Dipole-Gradient Optimization and Controlled Validation
We further demonstrate dipole-moment-enhanced polarization centers by systematically reducing dipole magnitude to achieve peak piezoelectric response. Crucially, we designed a control COF lacking polarization centers, confirming their necessity – an approach unreported in prior studies (including our own).
Conclusion: These combined strategies (BT integration, dipole engineering, experimental validation, and controlled comparison) represent a previously unexplored paradigm in piezoelectric COF design, solidifying the novelty of our contribution.
(4) Performance Comparison and Scope Clarification
We address performance benchmarks and material scope as follows:
(a) Direct Comparison under Matched Conditions
While conjugated microporous polymers Zn-Salen-TEPT (ACS Catal. 2024, 14, 7853) reports higher piezocatalytic H and H O yield (3260.2 μmol g-1 h-1 and 1569.8 μmol g-1 h-1) at 200 W ultrasound, our material (TP-BT-0F-COF) achieves exceptional piezo-photocatalytic synergy (2773.2 μmol g-1 h-1 for H and2735.5 for H O ) under lower energy input (120 W, 40 kHz) and dual stimuli.
(b) Specific Focus on COF-Based Systems
Our original statement explicitly references COF-based materials for piezo-photocatalytic both H and H O production. To date, only our prior work and this study reports such systems for both H and H O generation. Cited Angewandte studies (Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202420218, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, 64, e202419867) focus on H O production – a distinct application with different optimization targets (selectivity/yield/stability).
(c) Enhanced Rigor via Benchmarking
We have revised contentious phrasing as suggested and included Table S6 (Supplementary Materials) providing comprehensive benchmarking against state-of-the-art systems to ensure precision.
(5) Correction of Citation Issues
We sincerely apologize for citation inaccuracies and have implemented the following corrections:
(a) Reference 21: Removed from the subsequent section where it was misplaced. It was originally intended to support ‘element-regulated COF performance’ but was incorrectly positioned.
(b) References 23-24: Repurposed to support general principles of piezoelectric regulation (not our specific claims).
(c) Text revisions
The relevant section has been rewritten for enhanced rigor, with appropriate references reinserted to accurately reflect the literature context.
2. Technical:
1. Numerous studies have demonstrated that introducing fluorine (F) to modulate dipole moments in organic materials often results in positive regulation.
Dipole moments quantify the degree of charge separation between positive and negative charges, reflecting asymmetry in charge distribution at molecular or atomic scales. Mathematically, the dipole moment (μ) is defined as: μ= q d, where q is the charge magnitude and is the displacement vector from the negative to the positive charge.
The authors’ DFT computational model adopts a symmetric structure centered on the BT molecule. However, since their ligand modifications are solely based on the BT moiety, the inherent symmetry of this design diminishes the impact of molecular adjustments. For instance, in TP-SB-COF, the dipole moments from opposing sides are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, leading to negligible overall dipole moments in DFT calculations (Fig. 1). Using the molecular fragment within the red box in Figure 2 (one TP molecule connected to three BT molecules) for calculations can avoid the aforementioned issues.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestion to adopt an asymmetric molecular fragment model (one TP linked to three BT units) for dipole moment calculations. This revised approach effectively eliminates dipole cancellation artifacts inherent in symmetric full-unitcell models. Crucially, the new results validate our original findings:
(1) Fluorine Substitution Reduces Dipole Moments:
As shown in Fig. S40, the dipole moments follow: TP-BT-0F-COF: 1.420 D, TP-BT-1F-COF: 0.5995 D, TP-BT-2F-COF: 0.4416 D, TP-SB-COF: 0.013 D. The inverse correlation between F-content and μ confirms that F atoms competitively withdraw electron density from BT units, diminishing their electron-accepting capability and thus reducing molecular polarity.
(2) Mechanism of Dipole Suppression:
The strong electronegativity of F localizes electron density around itself, disrupting charge transfer along the BT-TP axis. This attenuates the overall charge separation vector (d in μ = q*d), explaining the reduction from 0F to 2F-COF.
(3) Role of β-Ketoenamine Linkages:
The higher μ of TP-BT-0F-COF (1.420 D) vs. BTA-BT-0F-COF (0.7476 D) underscores that β-ketoenamine motifs enhance polarization more effectively than BTA units by promoting asymmetric charge distribution.
2. The water oxidation reaction to produce H O should involve quenching •OH radicals, not holes (h⁺).
Response: We deeply appreciate the reviewer’s perceptive suggestions, which have substantially enhanced the mechanistic understanding of our study. To address these insights, isotopic labeling experiments for •OH trapping studies have been systematically executed, as elaborated below:
In order to investigate the water oxidation pathway, H 18O was employed as the reaction medium. The oxidation of benzoic acid produced p-hydroxybenzoic acid (p-HBA), with a characteristic mass peak at m/z = 139.0296 (Fig. S60). This signal corresponds to the 18O-labeled p-HBA adduct, substantiating that •OH radicals (and thus H O ) are derived from water oxidation. The reaction sequence is as follows: (H O + h+ → •OH + H+, 2.32 V vs NHE; 2•OH → H O , 0.74 V vs NHE)
(1) Charge Trapping Experiments Elucidate Oxidation Pathways:
To distinguish the roles of holes in the oxidation processes, scavenger-assisted studies were carried out:
(a) Hole Trapping and •OH Quenching (Oxidation Suppression):
Hole Scavenging: The introduction of 10 mM EDTA-2Na reduced H O yield by 87%, confirming that holes initiate the water oxidation step.
•OH Quenching: The addition of 10 vol% tert-butanol (TBA) resulted in an 91% decrease in H O production, further corroborating the dominance of •OH coupling in H O formation. These findings are in harmony with in situ ESR data (Fig. S59), where •OH signals were exclusively observed under piezo-photocatalytic conditions (ultrasound and light), but were absent under light alone.
(2) Summary of Mechanistic Insights
These integrated experiments provide definitive evidence that: H O forms through an indirect two-step water oxidation process involving hole-generated •OH radicals. Piezoelectric fields are indispensable for activating the water oxidation reaction (WOR) pathway, as corroborated by isotopic labeling (in situ ESR and MS) and charge-trapping kinetics.
3. While terephthalic acid is widely used to detect •OH radicals, its instability under light-ultrasound conditions compromises reliability. Additionally, the authors claim: ‘This may be because the COFs reduced the residual oxygen in the water to H O .’ This introduces ambiguity in experimental reproducibility and challenges the validity of •OH detection via terephthalic acid. Proper control experiments, such as isotopic labeling with H 18O, are critical to confirm that H O originates from water oxidation rather than oxygen reduction.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable concerns regarding 1) the suitability of terephthalic acid (TA) for •OH detection under combined light-ultrasound conditions and 2) the mechanistic ambiguity in H O generation. We have addressed these points as follows:
(1) Reliability of TA Probe
TA is a well-established •OH probe validated for piezo-photocatalytic systems. Previous studies confirm its stability under dual excitation within typical reaction duration (Adv. Mater. 2021, 33, 2101751). This is evidenced by: 1) Reproducible •OH quantification via TA fluorescence, 2) Direct correlation with in situ ESR signals (Fig. S59). 3) Isotopic labeling H 18O : Detection 18O-labeled p-hydroxybenzoic acid (m/z = 139.0296, Fig. S60). These three tests all confirm the generation of hydroxyl radicals, thereby further validating the reliability of the fluorescence produced by hydroxyl radical capture using TA. In addition, we conducted isotope tests with benzoic acid (which is similar to terephthalic acid), and the results can further demonstrate the stability of such substances after combining with hydroxyl radicals under piezo-photocatalytic conditions. This three-method validation ensures robust detection of water-oxidation-derived radicals.
(2) Clarification of H O Origin
We apologize for the unclear phrasing and now explicitly distinguish mechanisms:
(3) Photocatalysis (light only)
H O originates from oxygen reduction (ORR) by photogenerated electrons, consistent with: Weak TA-PL signals (Fig. S58), and thermodynamically inaccessible water oxidation (all COF valence bands < +2.32 V vs. NHE).
(4) Piezo-photocatalysis (light + ultrasound)
H O derives from water oxidation, confirmed by:
(a) Scavenger studies: H O production suppression with EDTA-2Na (hole scavenger) and TBA (•OH scavenger), indicating hole-mediated pathway: H O + h+ → •OH + H+, 2.32 V vs. NHE; 2•OH → H O , 0.74 V vs. NHE
(b) Isotopic labeling H 18O : Detection 18O-labeled p-hydroxybenzoic acid (m/z = 139.0296, Fig. S60), confirming •OH (and thus H O ) originates from water.
4. Lacking cyclic tests and characterization of the materials after reaction.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their valuable suggestion regarding cyclic stability testing and post-reaction characterization. In response, we have incorporated additional experimental data into the revised manuscript. While post-reaction XRD analysis revealed diminished peak intensities, the corresponding FTIR spectra (Fig. S53) remain nearly unchanged. This key observation confirms the robust structural integrity of the TP-BT-0F-COF framework throughout the piezo-photocatalytic process. Collectively, these results demonstrate the material's fundamental structural stability under reaction conditions.
5. Powdered materials cannot be directly tested for d coefficients using standard d meters. Supplementary Fig. S37 merely displays a photograph without detailing sample preparation or measurement protocols.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the challenges associated with measuring d coefficients in powdered materials. We acknowledge that standard d meters are optimized for dense, bulk samples and are not ideal for powdered specimens due to issues such as poor mechanical contact and non-uniform stress distribution. Regarding Supplementary Fig. S37, we agree that the original photograph alone was insufficient without detailed methodological context. To address this, we have now supplemented the manuscript with a comprehensive description of the sample preparation protocol.
6. The authors employed diamond anvil cells for characterization, but it remains unclear whether such extreme pressure conditions are relevant to practical piezoelectric catalysis. While similar methods are used in piezofluorochromism studies (e.g., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, e202409099), the connection between these fields and piezoelectric catalysis remains unexplained.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's insightful comment, which prompts us to clarify the rationale for employing diamond anvil cells (DAC) in our study. Based on the experimental data presented in the study, the use of DAC for high-pressure characterization serves as a powerful proxy to elucidate the intrinsic structure-property relationships governing piezoelectric response, even though the absolute pressures (GPa range) exceed those in practical piezocatalytic conditions. The relevance lies in the following aspects, supported by the data:
(1) Probing Polarization Sensitivity as a Signature of Piezoelectricity
In situ high-pressure FT-IR (Fig. 2D-E, S39) revealed that COFs with strong piezoelectricity exhibit significant blue shifts in β-ketoenamine units under pressure. Weakly piezoelectric/non-piezoelectric COFs (e.g., TP-SB-COF) showed minimal shifts. This demonstrates that pressure-induced bond polarization correlates directly with piezoelectric strength, as both arise from symmetry-breaking structural distortions.
(2) Bandgap Narrowing Under Pressure Mirrors Piezo-Potential Effects
In situ UV-Vis (Fig. 2F-H, S44-S49) showed that TP-BT-0F-COF’s bandgap narrowed by 0.47 eV (at 15 GPa), while weaker piezoelectrics (e.g., TP-BT-2F-COF) narrowed by only 0.36 eV. Bandgap reduction under pressure simulates the piezoelectric field-driven band bending in actual catalysis (Fig. 5G), which facilitates charge separation under mechanical stress. This was experimentally validated: samples with larger pressure-induced band shifts showed higher H /H O yields under ultrasound (Fig. 3A-E).
(3) Fluorescence Quenching Under Pressure Reflects Enhanced Charge Separation
In situ PL (Fig. 4A-B, S61-S62) revealed rapid fluorescence quenching in strongly piezoelectric COFs (e.g., TP-BT-0F-COF) under pressure, indicating suppressed charge recombination due to intensified π-π interactions and polarization. This parallels the ultrasound-driven charge separation in piezo-photocatalysis, where piezoelectric fields inhibit electron-hole recombination (Fig. 4B-C).
(4) Connection to Piezofluorochromism Studies
While piezofluorochromism focuses on pressure-induced emission shifts (e.g., Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2024, e202409099), this work extends the methodology to probe polarization-dependent electronic responses critical for catalysis. Both fields rely on high pressure to: (i) Amplify subtle structural distortions that induce dipole changes. (ii) Quantify how these distortions alter optoelectronic properties (bandgap, carrier mobility). The key difference: Piezofluorochromism tracks emission changes, whereas this study correlates pressure-driven structural/electronic responses with piezocatalytic activity.
(5) Why High Pressure is Mechanistically Relevant
Practical piezocatalysis operates at lower stresses, but the microscopic origin (symmetry-breaking → dipole alignment → charge separation) is identical. DAC experiments: Accelerate polarization effects to detectable levels. Rank materials by piezoelectric sensitivity (e.g., TP-BT-0F > TP-BT-2F). Validate DFT predictions of dipole moments (Fig. S41) and active sites (Fig. 5). Crucially, samples showing the largest high-pressure responses (TP-BT-0F-COF) delivered the best practical performance under ultrasound and light (Fig. 3C).
(6) Conclusion
High-pressure characterization is not a direct simulation of piezocatalytic conditions but an effective tool to decode the structure-polarization relationship. The study bridges these domains by showing that materials with high pressure sensitivity in bond polarization, bandgap narrowing, and carrier separation invariably exhibit superior piezocatalytic activity. This approach provides a molecular blueprint for designing high-performance piezocatalysts, where DAC experiments serve as a screening platform to identify candidates with robust dipole moments and polarization responses.
Thank you for your kind consideration.
Sincerely yours,
Jun-Min Liu

Response to Reviewers
Dear Reviewers,
Thanks very much for your comments. We have revised our manuscript “Enhanced piezo-photocatalytic water splitting activity via engineering robust dipole moments in covalent organic frameworks” according to your comments. The detailed point-by-point responses to the comments are listed as follows.
Reviewers’ comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
All my previous concerns have been satisfactorily resolved, and the manuscript is recommended to be accepted.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their positive feedback and endorsement.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I have no further questions.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their positive feedback and endorsement.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Comments:
The authors have clarified most of the experimental concerns expressed in the previous round of review. The observation of the SHG peak at 700 nm for the COF does indicate its non-centrosymmetric nature. However, the authors must recheck the space group of the material still. P1 is the most basic space group with no symmetry operations, which can be used to refine absolutely any material. It seems unlikely from the COF structure that it would possess no symmetry elements at all. Also, the chemical rationale behind symmetry breaking, be it torsion or twisting or rotation of the motifs, is still missing, which makes the structure-property correlations incomplete still.
Response:
1. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and for highlighting this critical point. The reviewer is absolutely correct that the P1 space group, due to its lack of symmetry, is often a starting point for refinement and may not reflect the true symmetry of a highly ordered COF structure. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have meticulously re-examined and re-refined the PXRD patterns for all COFs. The results conclusively demonstrate that a higher-symmetry space group provides an excellent fit to the experimental data. Specifically, the Pawley refinements were successfully performed in the following space groups, all of which yielded excellent agreement factors (Rwp and Rp < 10%): TP-BT-0F-COF and BTA-BT-0F-COF were refined in the P-6 space group. BT-1F-COF and TP-BT-2F-COF were refined in the P3 space group. The space groups of the above four COFs are all non-centrosymmetric. The space group P-3 of TP-SB-COF is centrosymmetric. This result is a directly quoted conclusion from relevant literature (Nature Chem 10, 1180-1189 (2018)). We have clearly marked the citation source in the subsequent supplementary materials to ensure the rigor of data traceability. Furthermore, fractional atomic coordinates for the unit cell of all COFs have been compiled and are presented in Tables S1-S5 in the Supporting Information. We believe that this revised structural assignment is now both physically reasonable and rigorously supported by the diffraction data. We are grateful to the reviewer for prompting this significant improvement to our work.
2. We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that a deeper mechanistic explanation of symmetry breaking is crucial for establishing robust structure-property relationships. In response, we have now revised the manuscript to provide a clearer chemical rationale, directly based on our experimental and computational data, which points to a combination of in-plane electronic polarization and bond-length alternation as the primary driver of symmetry breaking, rather than large-scale torsional or twisting motions. The key revisions and clarifications are as follows:
1) Electronic Asymmetry from the Donor-Acceptor (D-A) Motif: The primary source of symmetry breaking is the intrinsic electronic asymmetry of the benzothiadiazole (BT) unit. When linked to the electron-rich tri-phenylamine (TP) unit, it creates a strong D-A pair. This is evidenced by: (1) DFT-Calculated Dipole Moments： TP-BT-0F-COF, with the unmodified BT unit, possesses the largest dipole moment (1.420 D). Systematic fluorination, which tunes the BT unit's electron-withdrawing strength, progressively reduces this moment (TP-BT-1F-COF: 0.5995 D; TP-BT-2F-COF: 0.4416 D), directly linking molecular polarity to structure. (2) Optical Properties: The pronounced red-shift and narrower bandgap of TP-BT-0F-COF confirm strong intramolecular charge transfer, a hallmark of electronic symmetry breaking.
2) In-Plane Polarization from the β-Ketoenamine Linkage: The β-ketoenamine linkage enhances symmetry breaking not via torsion, but through its locked, planar conformation that enables inherent in-plane polarization. This is supported by: (1) In-situ High-Pressure FT-IR: Significant pressure-induced blue-shifts of C-N and C=C vibrations in β-ketoenamine-linked COFs (especially TP-BT-0F-COF) indicate bond shortening and intensified polarization. The absence of this effect in the imine-linked BTA-BT-0F-COF underscores its critical role. (2) Piezoelectric Tensor Analysis: DFT calculations confirm that the large piezoelectric tensor elements are primarily in-plane, with high Born effective charges (> |2.0 e|) localized near the β-ketoenamine group, identifying it as the key ‘piezoelectric active unit.’
3) Direct Experimental Confirmation: The macroscopic non-centrosymmetry resulting from this molecular-level design is unambiguously confirmed by: (1) Second-Harmonic Generation (SHG): A distinct SHG signal from TP-BT-0F-COF. (2) Violation of the Mutual Exclusion Rule: The concurrent appearance of specific vibrational modes in both IR and Raman spectra.
In summary, the symmetry breaking in TP-BT-0F-COF is driven by the synergy between the strong electronic asymmetry of the D-A BT motif and the in-plane polarization of the rigid β-ketoenamine linkage, creating a robust dipole moment that is the direct origin of its superior piezoelectric and piezo-photocatalytic performance. We have revised the manuscript to articulate this rationale clearly, ensuring a complete structure-property correlation.
Reviewer 4 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed the majority of my questions and concerns, with the exception of Comment 4 (Lacking cyclic tests). Nevertheless, I find the manuscript suitable for acceptance.
Response: We are deeply grateful to the reviewer for their positive assessment and for recommending our manuscript for acceptance.
Regarding Comment 4 on the lack of cyclic tests, we sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful point. At the outset of this study, we employed long-term stability tests as an alternative yet rigorous approach to demonstrate the robustness of our COF materials. Specifically, as shown in Supplementary Fig. S52, the COF maintained a high level of catalytic activity over a continuous 24-hour reaction period without significant decay. These long-term stability results indicate that the COF exhibited no notable activity attenuation and maintained structural stability during the continuous piezo-photocatalytic process. This aligns with the goal of verifying activity stability pursued by cyclic tests and thus also confirms its stable piezo-photocatalytic activity. We believe that this demonstrated long-term operational stability effectively proves that the COF maintains its structural integrity and catalytic activity over time, which is a crucial indicator of its practical application potential.
Thank you for your kind consideration.
Sincerely yours,
Jun-Min Liu
Professor in Chemistry
E-mail: liujunm@mail.sysu.edu.cn
School of Materials Science and Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University

## Paper

## Abstract

Covalent organic frameworks with tunable optical band gaps and notable piezoelectricity enable sustainable piezo-photocatalytic production of H2 and H2O2 via pure water splitting. Strong dipole moments can significantly boost piezoelectric properties, necessitating a systematic exploration of their structure-property relationships. Here, we synthesize a series of β-ketoenamine/imine-linked covalent organic frameworks, such as TP-BT-0F/1F/2F-COF, BTA-BT-0F-COF, and TP-SB-COF, through molecular design engineering. The combination of symmetry-breaking benzothiadiazole units and in-plane polarized β-ketoenamine linkages creates a robust dipole moment in TP-BT-0F-COF. This material demonstrates a high piezoelectric coefficient and band gap narrowing, achieving H2 and H2O2 production rates of 1501.4 and 1435.8 μmol g−1 h−1 under co-exposure to ultrasound (60 W, 40 kHz) and visible light. Density functional theory identifies N8 and C6 sites on benzothiadiazole units as potential catalytic sites for H2 and H2O2 evolution, respectively. Molecular design of covalent organic frameworks with prominent dipole moments advances mechano-optical energy conversion technologies.

---

## Introduction

Efficient water splitting to produce H2 and H2O2 is considered a potential green technology for converting renewable energy into other energy forms1. However, the photocatalytic water splitting reactions used for H2 production typically requires a sacrificial agents and/or co-catalysts2–4. Piezoelectric catalysis through the conversion of mechanical to chemical energy is a promising, environmentally friendly approach to the production of H2 and H2O2 5,6. In non-centrosymmetric crystalline materials, mechanical stress in piezoelectric catalysis generates polarized charges and built-in electric fields, driving charge carrier separation and inhibiting recombination7,8. Moreover, the piezoelectric-induced polarization drives band bending, promoting electron-hole separation, overcoming the thermodynamic barrier of water oxidation, and thus synergistically boosting catalytic efficiency9. A variety of piezoelectric materials, including BiFeO3, BaTiO3, and g-C3N4, have been utilized for water splitting to produce H2 and H2O2 via piezoelectricity10–14. However, classical inorganic piezoelectric materials are limited by poor structural tunability and complex polarization processes, which severely hamper their mechanically driven catalytic efficiency15. Consequently, the intrinsic structural tunability of framework materials establishes them as highly suitable candidates for emerging piezo-photocatalytic systems16–19.

Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as a paradigm-shifting photocatalytic platform. Their ordered nanoporosity and atomically precise structural programmability, achieved through modular covalent assembly, demonstrate their potential as pivotal visible-light-responsive photocatalysts20–22. Capitalizing on these programmable attributes, recent advances have exploited this design versatility to create two-dimensional (2D) COFs with engineered non-centrosymmetric frameworks, where symmetry-breaking polarization motifs synergistically enhance piezoelectric responses, thus expanding the scope of piezoelectric research23,24. For example, recent work engineered twistable bicarbazole motifs or fluorinated alkyl chains into COFs, enhancing piezoelectric performance25,26. Our prior work first reported that a highly crystalline β-ketoenamine-linked COF (EA-COF) could exhibit efficient piezo-photocatalytic H2 and H2O2 production in pure water without any co-catalyst. The piezoelectric properties of EA-COF were mainly attributed to the in-plane polarization of the β-ketoenamine groups within the framework27. At present, the structure-performance relationships dictating piezoelectricity in COFs are poorly understood. Thus, deliberate architectural tuning of piezo-photocatalytically tailored COFs requires systematic study to unravel critical design principles.

In this study, we rationally design and synthesize a series of β-ketoenamine/imine-linked BT-COFs exhibiting high piezo-photocatalytic activity through meticulous molecular engineering. The two critical factors governing the performance, such as in-plane polarization units and dipole moment, are systematically explored (Fig. 1). β-Ketoenamine-linked COFs exhibit piezoelectricity from ketoenamine unit in-plane polarization, whereas imine-linked COFs lacking these units have lower performance (Fig. 1A). Adjusting the dipole moment by introducing fluorine atoms or changing the structural unit affects the piezo-photocatalytic performance (Fig. 1B). Among them, TP-BT-0F-COF exhibits the highest piezo-photocatalytic water splitting efficiency, producing H2/H2O2 at rates of 1501.4/1435.8 μmol g−1 h−1 under ultrasound (60 W, 40 kHz) and visible light irradiation, respectively, and also shows good stability with H2/H2O2 production amounts of 18.9/14.5 mmol g−1 within 24 h. The enhanced performance arises from the synergy between ultrasound-induced polarized electric fields and the donor-acceptor benzothiadiazole (BT) unit design, which breaks symmetry to yield strong local dipole polarization. The N8 and C6 positions of the BT unit are also confirmed as the potential sites of H2 and H2O2 production by theoretical calculations, respectively. Experimental and computational analyses reveal that the BT-driven charge polarization mechanism enhances both photocatalytic efficiency and piezoelectric response, establishing a robust structure-property relationship for improved piezo-photocatalysis.
